UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

     PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                         )                Docket No. ER26-1088-000

             REQUEST FOR REHEARING OR, IN THE ALTERNATIVE,
        CLARIFICATION OF THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS

        Pursuant to Section 313 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)1 and Rules 212 and 713 of the

Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or

“FERC”),2 the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (“PJM Transmission Owners”)3 respectfully

request rehearing or, in the alternative, clarification of the Commission’s order on compliance

issued on April 16, 2026, in this proceeding.4

        In its December 18, 2025 order, the Commission found PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s

(“PJM”) Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) unjust and unreasonable because of a lack of

sufficient clarity or consistency as to the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to

 Interconnection Customers5 serving Co-Located Load.6 The Commission therefore directed PJM

to file within 30 days, as part of the replacement rate, revisions to the generation interconnection

procedures of the Tariff with respect to Interconnection Customers seeking to use new generating

facilities to serve Co-Located Load, including a definition of Co-Located Load.7

            On January 20, 2026, PJM submitted proposed revisions to its Tariff to comply with the

Commission’s requirement set forth in the December 18 Order.8 In the 30-Day Compliance Filing,

PJM proposed to add a definition of Co-Located Load to match defined terms in its Tariff9 and

proposed to define Co-Located Load based on facilities located on the customer’s side of the “Point

of Change in Ownership.”10 PJM explained that this revision was appropriate because the “Point

of Interconnection” could include connection to Transmission Owner Interconnection Facilities.11

            In the April 16 Compliance Order, the Commission accepted in part and rejected in part

PJM’s 30-Day Compliance Filing, effective April 16, 2026, and directed a further compliance

filing within 30 days.12 The Commission rejected PJM’s proposed definition of Co-Located Load

because PJM did not adopt the definition of Co-Located Load specified in the December 18 Order

and, according to the Commission, did not provide sufficient explanation for how PJM’s proposed

deviation complied with the Commission’s directive in the December 18 Order.13                                      The

 Commission therefore directed PJM to make a further compliance filing to revise the definition of

Co-Located Load in its Tariff to use the term “Point of Interconnection” instead of “Point of

Change in Ownership.”14

       The PJM Transmission Owners respectfully seek rehearing of that determination because

the Commission did not meaningfully engage with PJM’s explanation for using Point of Change

in Ownership. As PJM explained in its 30-Day Compliance Filing, the Point of Change in

Ownership is the more appropriate demarcation because it reflects the legal and operational

boundary between customer-owned facilities and Transmission Owner facilities and avoids

sweeping Transmission Owner interconnection facilities into the definition of Co-Located Load.15

Moreover, the Commission did not adequately address the practical consequences of using “Point

of Interconnection” instead of “Point of Change in Ownership” in the definition of Co-Located

Load, and incorrectly determined based on unsubstantiated allegations that the use of “Point of

Change in Ownership” could lead to “uncertainty or delays” for parties in Co-Located Load

configurations. The Commission should grant rehearing and permit PJM to define Co-Located

Load based on the Point of Change in Ownership

       If the Commission, however, declines to grant rehearing and continues to require the use

of “Point of Interconnection” in the definition of Co-Located Load, the PJM Transmission Owners

request that the Commission grant certain requested clarifications in Section II below to ensure

that the definition is not applied in a manner that creates operational confusion, threatens

reliability, or expands the new transmission services beyond the scope intended in the

Commission’s December 18 Order.

 I.     REQUEST FOR REHEARING

       A.       Statement of Issues and Specification of Errors.

       The PJM Transmission Owners submit the following Statement of Issues and Specification

of Errors pursuant to Rules 713(c)(1) and 713(c)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and

Procedure:16

       The April 16 Compliance Order is arbitrary and capricious, fails to reflect reasoned
       decision-making and is unsupported by substantial evidence in violation of the
       Administrative Procedure Act with respect to the definition of Co-Located Load because
       the Commission did not develop a sufficient record on which to base its definition of Co-
       Located Load, failed to fully consider the rationale provided by PJM for basing that
       definition on the Point of Change in Ownership, and rendered a decision based on
       unsubstantiated allegations of discrimination. Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm
       Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983); Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y. v. FERC, 45 F.4th
       265 (D.C. Cir. 2022); Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y. v. FERC, 347 F.3d 964, 972 (D.C. Cir.
       2003); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 161 FERC ¶ 61,252 (2017); PJM Interconnection,
       L.L.C., 119 FERC ¶ 61,318 (2007); Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 117
       FERC ¶ 61,113 (2006).

       B.       Argument.

                1.        The Commission Failed to Meaningfully Consider the Explanation for
                          Proposing a Definition of Co-Located Load Based on Point of Change
                          in Ownership.

       In its 30-Day Compliance Filing, PJM proposed to define Co-Located Load based on

facilities located on the customer’s side of the “Point of Change in Ownership.”17 PJM explained

that using the Point of Change in Ownership is the more appropriate demarcation point, as opposed

to the Point of Interconnection, because it avoids including facilities owned by Transmission

Owners in the definition of Co-Located Load facilities.18 PJM further explained in its 60-Day

Compliance Filing that the “Point of Change in Ownership” is the more precise and administrable




16
       18 C.F.R. § 385.713(c)(1), (c)(2).
17
       30-Day Compliance Filing at 3 & n.14.
18
       Id. at 3 & n.14.



                                                4
 boundary because it identifies the legal and operational demarcation between facilities owned by

the project developer and facilities owned by the Transmission Owner.19 In addition, PJM

explained that using the “Point of Change in Ownership” better aligns the Tariff with PJM’s

current interconnection terminology, provides greater clarity to interconnection parties concerning

the facilities to which Co-Located Load may attach, and avoids disputes over whether

Transmission Owner-owned facilities fall within the Co-Located Load configuration.20

        The April 16 Compliance Order did not meaningfully address PJM’s explanation. Instead,

the Commission rejected PJM’s proposed use of “Point of Change in Ownership” largely because

the December 18 Order referred to “Point of Interconnection,” and the Commission’s conclusion

that PJM had not sufficiently explained why it deviated from that language in the 30-Day

Compliance Filing.21 But that reasoning does not address the merits of PJM’s concern. PJM was

not proposing a stylistic change. It was identifying a substantive problem with using “Point of

Interconnection” as the operative boundary in the definition of Co-Located Load—namely, that

the term could sweep in Transmission Owner facilities that are not properly part of the customer’s

co-located configuration.

        That issue matters because the potential inclusion of Transmission Owner-owned facilities

within the definition of Co-Located Load could improperly expand access to the new transmission

services adopted in the December 18 Order to load and generation facilities that are not truly

located at the same site, and indeed may not even be affiliated or have any contractual relationship.


19
         See id.; see also PJM 60-Day Compliance Filing, Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 32 (filed Feb. 23, 2026)
(“60-Day Compliance Filing”). Although PJM filed the 60-Day Compliance Filing in a separate docket, the
Commission can and should have considered the explanation provided therein, as it bears on the same definitional
issue as raised in the 30-Day Compliance Filing docket, both of which stem from the Commission’s December 18
Order.
20
        60-Day Compliance Filing at 32-34.
21
        See April 16 Compliance Order at P 27.

 In the December 18 Order, the Commission established a new framework under which an Eligible

Customer may take one of three transmission services on behalf of Co-Located Load.22 It is

reasonable to limit that framework to bona fide co-location arrangements—i.e., arrangements

involving generation and load that are meaningfully co-located and can be studied, planned, and

served under rules tailored to that configuration.

       But if the definition of Co-Located Load turns on the Point of Interconnection, parties may

attempt to rely on Transmission Owner-owned facilities located on the customer’s side of the Point

of Interconnection to argue that generation and load are sufficiently co-located to qualify for the

new transmission services, even where the relevant customer facilities are not actually at the same

site. This is because the Point of Change in Ownership is often located closer to the customer’s

facility than the Point of Interconnection. The figures below demonstrate two such configurations.

In these configurations, the red lines represent network transmission facilities owned by a

Transmission Owner, the green lines represent interconnection facilities owned by the

Transmission Owner, and the black lines represent customer-owned facilities.23




22
       December 18 Order at PP 2, 193.
23
       Metering would be located on the customer-side of the Point of Interconnection.

                                                      Figure 1




        As Figure 1 demonstrates,24 an entity could attempt to use the location of Transmission

Owner-owned facilities relative to the Point of Interconnection to claim that its load qualifies as

Co-Located Load, and therefore that it is entitled to one of the new transmission services, even

though the arrangement does not reflect a true same-site co-location of customer generation and

load. The customer could attempt to point to Transmission Owner-owned facilities on the

customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection and argue that due to those facilities it satisfies the

definition of Co-Located Load, even though the arrangement does not involve generation and load




24
         To be clear, as discussed below, the PJM Transmission Owners do not believe that it is appropriate to add
load as indicated in this figure without including protection at the generator step-up transformer, but are concerned
that customers could avoid an obligation to include such protection due to defining Co-Located Load based on the
Point of Interconnection.


                                                         7
 that are connected by any customer-owned facilities, and indeed, does not even involve facilities

that are located at the same site.25

        This could even extend to situations in which the generator and load have no relationship

at all, and a load simply wishes to take advantage of one of the new transmission services intended

exclusively for Co-Located Load. This type of situation is shown in Figure 2 below, where a third-

party load is not affiliated and has no contractual relationship with the load or generation in a Co-

Located Load arrangement, but nevertheless claims eligibility to take one of the new transmission

services due to the fact that it is “physically connected” to the generator through the Transmission

Owner-owned interconnection facility.

                                                  Figure 2




25
         The PJM Transmission Owners do not believe that the Commission intended to permit Co-Located Load
arrangements where there is no customer-owned facility physically connecting the end-use customer load and “co-
located” generation. At a minimum, the Commission should clarify that such arrangements do not qualify as Co-
Located Load. Alternatively, the Commission should grant rehearing for the reasons discussed herein.



                                                      8
         These types of gamesmanship would undermine the administrability of the Commission’s

new framework, blur the distinction between customer-owned and Transmission Owner-owned

facilities, and invite disputes over eligibility for the new services. They would also be contrary to

the Commission’s stated objective of bringing greater clarity and consistency to PJM’s Tariff rules

for co-location arrangements.26 The December 18 Order likewise emphasized the importance of

accommodating co-location arrangements in a manner that preserves reliability and avoids

inefficient outcomes.27 If entities are permitted to stretch the definition of Co-Located Load by

relying on Transmission Owner-owned facilities that happen to fall on the customer’s side of the

Point of Interconnection, the new transmission services could be used in circumstances for which

they were not intended, to the detriment of both efficiency and reliability.

        The Commission needs to account for these consequences in deciding the just and

reasonable definition of Co-Located Load.                Rehearing is therefore warranted because the

Commission failed to engage in reasoned decision-making. To satisfy its obligation to engage in

reasoned decision-making, the Commission must examine the relevant data and articulate a

rational connection between the facts found and the choices made.28 The Commission must reach

its conclusion through decision-making that is “reasoned, principled, and based upon the record”29

and, if the Commission “does not provide a rational explanation for its action based on the relevant

1021, 1030 (D.C. Cir. 1987)); Colo. Interstate Gas Co. v. FERC, 146 F.3d 889, 893 (D.C. Cir. 1998).

 data, then that action is arbitrary and capricious.”30 To avoid an arbitrary and capricious decision

or one that does not reflect reasoned decision-making, the Commission must consider all important

aspects of the problem at issue.31 And it is “well established that the Commission must ‘respond

meaningfully to the arguments raised before it.’”32

         PJM’s proposal to use “Point of Change in Ownership” directly addressed the risk that the

Co-Located Load definition could be manipulated through reliance on Transmission Owner-

owned facilities, thereby expanding the new transmission services beyond their intended scope in

the December 18 Order and potentially resulting in gaming of the Co-Located Load process to the

detriment of efficiency and reliability.             Because the April 16 Compliance Order did not

meaningfully consider PJM’s explanation for the use of “Point of Change in Ownership” in the

30-Day Compliance Filing, the Commission’s rejection of PJM’s proposed definition does not

reflect reasoned decision-making.33

                  2.       Using Point of Interconnection as a Metric to Determine What
                           Constitutes Co-Located Load Will Create Confusion Regarding
                           Responsibility for Protection System Arrangements and the Scope of
                           Eligibility for the new Transmission Services.

         The record does not support the Commission’s directive to use “Point of Interconnection”

as the operative boundary in the definition of Co-Located Load without further analysis. As PJM

explained, use of Point of Interconnection can create ambiguity because, in some configurations,

Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n, 463 U.S. at 43)).
31

FERC must more fully explain its decision).
32

33
         See 30-Day Compliance Filing at 3 & n.14.



                                                         10
 facilities on the customer’s side of that point may nonetheless include Transmission Owner-owned

facilities.34 That ambiguity has several important consequences that the April 16 Compliance

Order did not adequately address.

       The use of Point of Interconnection creates practical confusion regarding protection

responsibilities, including the location of required Protection System arrangements, responsibility

for maintaining them, and ownership of associated protection equipment where facilities on the

customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection remain owned by the Transmission Owner.

Defining Co-Located Load by reference to the “Point of Interconnection” may create confusion in

some configurations as to where the relevant facilities are located for purposes of protection

obligations and, correspondingly, which party bears responsibility for installing, maintaining, and

operating appropriate Protection Systems. It also may create confusion regarding ownership of

the protection equipment itself. If Co-Located Load is defined to include facilities located on the

customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection, parties could incorrectly assume that the protection

associated with those facilities is also customer-owned. But in some configurations, facilities

located on the customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection may nonetheless remain

Transmission Owner-owned. In those circumstances, use of the Point of Interconnection as the

definitional boundary could create uncertainty as to who owns the related protection equipment

and, correspondingly, who is responsible for installing, operating, maintaining, testing, repairing,

and replacing that protection.

       That distinction matters, particularly with respect to existing generation facilities. Existing

generation facilities often have equipment configurations whereby the facility lacks transmission-

level breakers on the high side of the generator step-up transformer, in which cases the breakers in


34
        Id.



                                                 11
 the substation at the Point of Interconnection must operate to address any generation faults. In this

situation, defining the Co-Located Load as including any facilities up to the Point of

Interconnection would create uncertainty as to the relative responsibilities of the Transmission

Owner and customer. This is because including Transmission Owner-owned facilities, such as

substation breakers, within the scope of the Co-Located Load arrangement could be used to attempt

to compel a Transmission Owner to take on the responsibility for protecting the customer’s

generator step-up transformer, or to prevent a Transmission Owner from installing and operating

adequate protection systems in order to ensure the protection of its network facilities beyond the

Point of Interconnection.

       Nothing in the December 18 Order suggests that the Commission intended the definitional

use of “Point of Interconnection” to function as a substitute for the separate engineering,

ownership, and operational determinations that govern Protection Systems. Nor did the April 16

Compliance Order state that replacing “Point of Change in Ownership” with “Point of

Interconnection” was intended to determine ownership of protection equipment, reallocate

responsibility for such equipment, or diminish a Transmission Owner’s ability to protect its

facilities. Rather, the April 16 Compliance Order addressed only whether PJM had complied with

the Commission’s directive to use the Commission-adopted definition.

       Defining Co-Located Load arrangements based on the Point of Interconnection also has

the potential to create complexity and confusion regarding the respective security responsibilities

between customers and Transmission Owners with respect to substation facilities, and will make

tracking North American Electric Reliability Corporation compliance obligations more difficult.

The April 16 Compliance Order did not meaningfully consider and address these consequences.

Instead, it concluded only that PJM had not sufficiently justified departing from the Commission-




                                                 12
 directed wording in a compliance filing and that PJM’s proposed modification might lead to

uncertainty or delay.35 That reasoning does not adequately respond to PJM’s explanation or

resolve the practical problems created by use of “Point of Interconnection” in the definition of Co-

Located Load.

       The simplest and most straightforward solution is for the Commission to grant rehearing

and permit PJM to use “Point of Change in Ownership” in the definition of Co-Located Load.

That approach would align the definition with the legal and operational boundary between

customer-owned facilities and Transmission Owner-owned facilities, avoid disputes over whether

Transmission Owner facilities fall within the Co-Located Load configuration, and better reflect

PJM’s existing interconnection terminology.36 However, if the Commission decides to retain

“Point of Interconnection,” it should grant the requested clarifications discussed below to ensure

the definition of Co-Located Load does not threaten reliability or undermine the efficient

interconnection of Co-Located Load arrangements.

                3.       The Commission’s Decision Incorrectly Relied on Speculative
                         Assertions of Potential Inefficiency

       The Commission’s decision to reject PJM’s proposed definition of Co-Located Load was

based in part on its conclusion that “the record here suggests PJM’s proposed modification to this

definition may lead to uncertainty or delays for parties in Co-Located Load configurations.”37 The

opposite is true. For the reasons explained above, basing the definition of Co-Located Load on

the Point of Interconnection is likely to create confusion, uncertainty and disputes potentially

resulting in delays in interconnecting Co-Located Load arrangements, particularly for

Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) are based on nothing more than

speculative assertions of potential Transmission Owner discrimination based on a fictitious animus

that Transmission Owners allegedly have for Co-Located Load arrangements.38 The sum of

Constellation’s “proof” of such intended discrimination is based on an unsupported allegation

regarding a single conversation with one Transmission Owner regarding ownership of certain ring

bus facilities,39 which Constellation generalizes into an imagined hostility to Co-Located Load

arrangements on the part of all Transmission Owners. Such unsupported allegations fall far below

the standard of substantial evidence necessary to support the Commission’s decision to reject

PJM’s proposed definition of Co-Located Load.40

II.      REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION IN THE ALTERNATIVE

         If the Commission declines to grant rehearing as requested above, the PJM Transmission

Owners respectfully request the Commission clarify the definition of Co-Located Load in April

16 Order. These clarifications are necessary if the definition of Co-Located Load relies on “Point

of Interconnection” for purposes of eligibility for the new transmission services, because that

definition: (i) obscures the obligations and responsibilities of Transmission Owners and customers,

respectively own; and (ii) opens to the door to potential gamesmanship by customers taking

advantage of Co-Located Load arrangements based on the inclusion or use of Transmission-

Owner-owned facilities.

        A.      The Commission Should Clarify That the use of “Point of Interconnection” in
                the Definition of Co-Located Load Does not Alter or Obscure Transmission
                Owners’ and Customer’s Obligations and Responsibilities With Respect to
                Protection Schemes.

        The Commission should clarify that use of “Point of Interconnection” in the definition of

Co-Located Load does not dilute or undermine the parties’ obligations with respect to Protection

Systems.     If the Commission continues to use “Point of Interconnection” as the relevant

definitional metric for determining eligibility for the new transmission services established in the

December 18 Order, that definition is not a proxy for allocating responsibility for Protection

Systems and cannot obscure the distinct obligations that the Transmission Owner and the customer

have with respect to their respective facilities.

        Clarification is necessary because, in some configurations, facilities located on the

customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection may nonetheless remain Transmission Owner-

owned. In those circumstances, as discussed above, use of the Point of Interconnection as the

definitional boundary may create confusion regarding where protection is required, which party is

responsible for installing and maintaining that protection, and who owns the associated protection

equipment. The Commission therefore should clarify that the definition of Co-Located Load using

“Point of Interconnection” does not affect either: (1) the customer’s obligation to design, install,

operate, and maintain appropriate protection on customer-owned facilities; or (2) the Transmission

Owner’s right to require, install, operate, and maintain appropriate protection on Transmission




                                                    15
 Owner-owned facilities.41 Consistent with PJM’s and the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposals,

the Commission should not permit the definition of Co-Located Load to negate a requirement for

necessary redundancy.42

         The Commission should also clarify that the definition of Co-Located Load that includes

“Point of Interconnection” should not impact the obligations of the customer or the rights of the

Transmission Owner to install appropriate Protection Systems, regardless of where the Point of

Change in Ownership or Point of Interconnection is located for any particular Co-Located Load

arrangement.

         B.      If the Commission Retains “Point of Interconnection” in the Definition of Co-
                 Located Load, it Should Clarify That Transmission-Owner-Owned Facilities
                 on the Customer Side of the Interconnection are not Part of the Co-Located
                 Load Arrangement.

Ownership” is the more appropriate demarcation point because it avoids including facilities owned

by Transmission Owners in the definition of Co-Located Load facilities.43                         However, the

Commission’s December 18 Order adopted a definition of Co-Located Load using the “Point of

Interconnection,” and the April 16 Compliance Order directed PJM to retain that phrase rather than

substitute “Point of Change in Ownership.”44 But without further clarification, parties may attempt

to rely on Transmission Owner-owned facilities located on the customer’s side of the Point of

Interconnection to claim eligibility for the new transmission services established by the December

 18 Order where the generation and load are not meaningfully co-located at the same site, and even

in cases where the generator and load are not affiliated and have no contractual relationship.

       That concern is not merely theoretical. Without PJM’s proposed modification to the

definition of Co-Located Load to use “Point of Change in Ownership” rather than “Point of

Interconnection,” this could invite entities to exploit certain interconnection configurations in

order to expand the availability of the new transmission services beyond the scope the Commission

intended in the December 18 Order. This concern is discussed in greater detail in Section I.

       The same ambiguity could also create confusion as to whether an entity qualifies to receive

transmission service at all. Regardless of how Co-Located Load is defined, an entity must still

satisfy the PJM Tariff’s separate definition of Eligible Customer in order to take any transmission

service. Absent clarification, some entities may attempt to invoke the Co-Located Load definition

as a substitute for satisfying the separate Eligible Customer requirements in the PJM Tariff.

Indeed, some entities have argued in these proceedings that any load located in PJM should have

ability to take the new services designed exclusively for co-located load arrangements.45 This

outcome would be inconsistent with the Commission’s December 18 Order, which addressed

transmission service for facilities that are both co-located and served through an Eligible Customer

under the PJM Tariff. It could also create the risk of unauthorized retail wheeling. A load customer

might, for instance, argue that it is eligible to receive one or more of the new transmission services

because it meets the definition of Co-Located Load simply due to being connected to a generator

through a facility behind the Point of Interconnection. This could be the case even if the load does

 not meet the definition of an Eligible Customer under the PJM Tariff, e.g., because it is located in

       Clarification is warranted given the Commission’s legitimate concerns regarding the

reliability impacts of significant amounts of “behind the meter” load.46 In light of these concerns,

it makes little sense to leave unresolved an ambiguity that could allow parties to argue that

Transmission Owner-owned facilities are part of a Co-Located Load arrangement solely because

       Accordingly, if the Commission continues to require use of “Point of Interconnection”

rather than PJM’s proposed “Point of Change in Ownership” in the definition of Co-Located Load,

it should clarify that Transmission Owner-owned facilities are not part of the Co-Location

arrangement merely because they are located on the customer’s side of the Point of

Interconnection. The Commission should also clarify that customers may not rely on Transmission

Owner-owned facilities, or other third-party-owned facilities with which the customer has no

contractual arrangement, to satisfy the definition of Co-Located Load. Finally, the Commission

should clarify that even if a customer meets the definition of Co-Located Load based on the

location of the Point of Interconnection, that customer must separately meet the definition of

Eligible Customer in order to take one of the new transmission services.
